title: None worse than me
hookLine: a Kabir couplet: I went looking for a bad man and found none worse than myself
tomorrow: Kabir says a moon shines in his body. why can't he see it?

lines: I WENT LOOKING FOR THE BAD ONE.
cards: Zoe said it at lunch, loud enough for the whole break room: Theo's family is so judgmental. Then she heard herself. Kabir has two lines for exactly that moment, and in Hindi they go like this.
Bura jo dekhan main chala, bura na milya koy. Jo dil khoja apna, mujhsa bura na koy. I went out looking for the bad one, and found no one bad.
Then I searched my own heart: there's no one worse than me.

teach.h: A DOHA: TWO LINES, BUILT TO BE SUNG.
teach.b: That's a doha: two lines, each with a little pause in the middle, built to be remembered and sung. His couplets have another name in his tradition, sakhis, which means witnesses.

teach.h: SAKHI: A WITNESS YOU TEST ON YOUR LIFE.
teach.b: A sakhi is something you test on your own life. And this one is a whole story in two lines. A man sets out to find the bad people of the world.
He walks the streets and comes back empty. Then he turns around, looks inside, and finds the one he was hunting. Kabir has a second couplet that goes with it.
Keep your critic close, he says, build him a hut in your own courtyard. Without water, without soap, he washes your nature clean.

And in the Guru Granth Sahib a saying of Kabir's goes further: I am the worst of all; everyone else is good. This is a real teaching of bhakti, devotion: the lover of God starts by lowering himself, not the neighbor.
It's about where to look first.
Kabir's dohas are sharp with priests and pandits, but this one he aims at the mirror.

how: Kabir's dohas are learned by heart and sung in bhajan gatherings; Sikhs sing his saloks from the Guru Granth Sahib in kirtan.

o: a temple hymn with a refrain repeated many times
a short prose saying written on a palm leaf
a two-line couplet made to be remembered and sung

games.q: the couplets and what they say: tap the pairs.
p: two lines, a pause in each, made to sing
a witness you test on your own life
keep him close; he washes you clean
out in the streets, then home to the heart

s: a doha is a long hymn sung in temples
it's a two-line couplet with a pause in each line, built to be remembered.
Kabir says to keep critics far away so they can't hurt you
build your critic a hut in your own courtyard: he washes your nature clean.
Kabir's couplets are also called sakhis, witnesses
a sakhi is something you test on your own life.

games.q: your roommate complains for ten minutes about a coworker. you start to agree. what would Kabir's doha do first?
o: add your own story about the coworker
tell the roommate she's the problem
check your own heart for the same fault
games.why: Kabir went looking for the bad one, came home, and searched his own heart first. none worse than me.

practice: Tap the doha's beat on your knee, and say it out loud, slowly: bura jo dekhan main chala, bura na milya koy. Then rest your hand on your chest and say the second line, jo dil khoja apna, mujhsa bura na koy.
Let the rest of the time be quiet, with the hand still there.

wordCard.voice: Doha: a two-line couplet with a pause in each line, made to be remembered and sung. Kabir's are short enough to carry by heart.

orig.note: Hindi: a couplet of two lines, each split by a pause; Kabir's are short enough to carry by heart.

carryVoice: Pocket this: none worse than me, the place Kabir looked first. Half of Kabir's week, done.
